title: Unit economics & performance brief — draft
body:
Context:
We need a concise messaging pack for sales, the website hero bullets, and a short one-pager the solutions team can use when customers ask: 'How are you faster and cheaper than the managed endpoints / self-hosted stacks we evaluate?'

Goal:
- Create defensible, testable claims about latency and per-token economics that map to specific assets (benchmarks, methodology writeups, reproducible scripts).
- Provide copy variants for hero, datasheet bullet, and salesperson soundbites.
- Flag any claims that need legal/bench review before public use.

Audience:
- Platform/infra engineering buyers (SRE, infra eng) focused on latency and predictable throughput
- ML engineers evaluating tradeoffs between hosted APIs and self-hosted inference stacks
- Technical evaluators at startups/enterprises comparing unit cost across vendors

Key messaging primitives (working drafts):
1) Hero headline (short):
   - "Predictable latency. Half the token cost. One inference platform."
   - Alternate: "Ship LLM features with predictable performance and better unit economics."

2) Subhead / supporting bullets (datasheet style):
   - "P50/P95 latency claims backed by internal benchmarks and customer pilots; automatic fallback when capacity constrained."
   - "Workload-aware batching + KV cache reduces per-token compute by up to 40% on common chat workloads."
   - "Quantization & kernel selection choices cut GPU memory and cost while preserving output quality for production workloads."

Core quantitative claims (draft, require bench verification):
- Typical chat workload (512 tokens, streaming, batch=8): P95 latency = ~120 ms on our Dedicated instance vs ~240 ms on competitive managed endpoints in our controlled benchmark (same model family, comparable GPU class).
- Unit cost (tokens processed) in production-like traces: 30–55% lower total compute cost vs unmanaged self-hosted baseline when using Redwood Optimize suggestions (batching + prefix caching + q4 quantization).
- Autoscaling + reserved capacity reduces tail latency variability by ~2x for bursty conversational traffic in customer pilots.

Methodology summary (for appendix and reproducibility):
- Models: open-family 13B-ish and 33B-ish variants that customers commonly deploy (quantized where noted).
- Workloads: 3 synthetic traces derived from customer anonymized traces — lightweight chat (avg length 64), conversational (avg length 512), long-form completion (avg length 2048).
- Hardware: A100-equivalent and H100-equivalent baselines, same instance SKU where possible; use CUDA kernels matched to model arch.
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency for first and last token, tokens/sec throughput, end-to-end token cost (GPU time * price + infra overhead).
- Isolation: Tests run in single-tenant reserved pools to avoid noisy neighbor effects; competitor numbers measured in their managed endpoints in same region when allowed.

Proof points / experimental highlights (narrative form for sales):
- Prefix caching case: for chat sessions with repeated system prompts / personas we saw effective per-request GPU-time drop of 25–40% (depends on prompt length), directly translating into lower per-token bill.
- Adaptive batching: small latency-sensitive requests are sent to low-latency pools while background bulk requests get high-batch, high-throughput lanes — net effect: maintain p95 SLOs while improving token efficiency over a single-tier approach.
- Quantization profile: q4_1 quantization for 13B models gave <2% measured quality delta on our automated eval prompts while lowering GPU memory footprint enough to double packing density on certain instance types.

Competitive positioning bullets (talking points):
- Versus big-cloud managed endpoints: Redwood provides comparable API simplicity but with deeper workload optimizations (KV caching, adaptive batching) and the option for Dedicated/Private deployments that keep latency predictable; we offset higher marginal infra cost by better packing/quantization.
- Versus open-source self-hosted stacks: self-hosting can be cheaper at infinite ops scale but has high ops burden and unpredictable tail latency; Redwood gives the ops guarantees and autoscaling primitives while still enabling comparable unit economics through Optimize.
- Versus pure inference vendors: our product is an opinionated platform with rollout/observability tooling (trace-level latency + token-cost breakdown) — not just a runtime. This reduces time-to-production and regression risk.

Copy for elevator pitches (30s):
- Sales: "With Redwood you get lower and more predictable latency plus fewer compute hours per token. That means better end user experience and lower monthly cloud spend — usually 30–50% lower compute spend versus the most common self-hosted patterns we see in customers."
- Technical AE: "We measure both latency and token economics. By combining prefix caching, batching, and quantization choices tuned per model, we provide demonstrable unit cost reductions while keeping p95 latency within your SLOs."

Risks / caveats to surface (must be included on external collateral if quantitative claims used):
- Benchmarks depend heavily on model family, sequence length distribution, and instance class — include full methodology link and dataset traces when publishing numbers.
- Customer mileage will vary; we should use phrasing like 'typical chat workloads in our benchmark suite' and avoid absolute 'always' statements.
- Any direct competitor comparisons must be validated against public pricing and have a review from legal/bench team.

Assets to produce before public rollout (action items):
- Final bench runs for the three traces (owner: Ravi) — reproducible scripts, raw logs, aggregated report (GH + Confluence).
- One-pager datasheet with hero, 3 proof bullets, methodology link, and an FAQ (owner: Aisha).
- Slide pack for AEs with talking points, one example customer pilot, and a short demo script (owner: Daniel).
- Legal/bench review checkpoint to sign off on numeric claims and competitor comparisons (owner: Sofia).

Open questions / discussion points:
- Do we want to use absolute percentage ranges (e.g., 30–55%) or stick to single-number conservative claims? Preference from sales: ranges are more flexible; legal prefers conservative single numbers backed by reproducible tests.
- Which competitor(s) do we name explicitly in external collateral? (Suggestion: cite anonymized 'leading managed API' in public materials; use direct comparisons in deal docs only after bench sign-off.)

Appendix (quick references):
- Benchmark repo: github.com/redwood-inference/benchmarks (see chat-latency-runbook.md)
- Internal confluence: confluence.redwood/benchmarks/unit-econ-2024
- Related tickets: jira GTMP-1123 (messaging brief), INFRA-2048 (batching infra improvements)

Notes to self:
- Keep the hero short and benefit-led; technical proof belongs in.datasheet + appendix.
- Make sure every numeric claim links to a single bench artifact that reproduces it.

End of draft.
